subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive an expression for the potential energy of an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field.

verification.note: The 1+2+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). Hand-checked: τ = qE·2a sin θ = pE sin θ; ∫sin θ dθ = −cos θ gives W = pE(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂); the reference θ₁ = 90° gives the standard U = −pE cos θ. The book prints the same chain (its lowercase u and capital PE written here as U and pE).

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The torque
lines: A dipole of moment p = q·2a is placed in a
uniform field E, with p at an angle θ to E.
The equal and opposite forces +qE and −qE
form a couple. Its torque is

lines.text: τ = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ

steps.margin_note: First mark. Force times perpendicular separation: qE times 2a sin θ.
steps.why: The two forces cancel as a net force but act along different lines; the perpendicular distance between those lines is 2a sin θ, so the pair turns the dipole instead of moving it.
common_mistakes: Writing cos θ in the torque. The turning arm is the PERPENDICULAR separation, 2a sin θ.
Adding the two forces to get a net force. They cancel; only the torque remains.

recall.must_convey: That the two forces qE form a couple with torque pE sin theta.
reject: work is pE cos theta one minus cos theta two

steps.memory_tip: Torque takes sin θ; the energy result takes cos θ. Sin turns, cos stores.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: The dipole at angle θ to the field, the two opposite forces, and the dashed perpendicular separation 2a sin θ.
steps.why: The dashed drop from +q to the line of the −q force IS the torque arm — seeing it as a length is what makes τ = qE × 2a sin θ readable instead of memorised.
common_mistakes: Drawing the two forces along the dipole axis. They are along the FIELD, one each way.

recall.must_convey: That the dipole is drawn at angle theta to the field with forces qE each way and the separation 2a sin theta marked.
accept: draw the dipole at theta to the field

steps.memory_tip: Tilted rod, two opposite arrows along the field, one dashed drop for the arm.

steps.label: The work integral
lines: To rotate the dipole through a small angle dθ
against this torque, the work needed is

lines.text: dW = τ dθ = pE sin θ dθ

lines: Rotating from angle θ₁ to θ₂ with the field:

lines.text: W = pE ∫ sin θ dθ, θ from θ₁ to θ₂
W = pE [−cos θ] from θ₁ to θ₂

steps.margin_note: Two marks. The integral of sin θ is −cos θ; the limits θ₁ to θ₂ must be shown.
steps.why: The torque changes as the angle changes, so the work must be integrated over the angle; the minus from ∫sin θ dθ = −cos θ is what puts cos θ₁ FIRST in the bracket.
common_mistakes: Writing cos θ₂ − cos θ₁. The integral's minus sign reverses the order.
Integrating to +cos θ instead of −cos θ.
Using force times distance — a rotation stores work through torque times angle.

recall.must_convey: That dW = pE sin theta d-theta is integrated from theta-one to theta-two, giving pE into cos theta-one minus cos theta-two.
accept: integrate pE sin theta d theta
from theta one to theta two
cos theta one minus cos theta two

steps.memory_tip: ∫sin = −cos, and that minus flips the limits: θ₁'s cosine comes first.

steps.label: The potential energy
lines: This work is stored as the potential energy
Measured from the reference θ₁ = 90°, the
potential energy at angle θ is U = −pE cos θ.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Box the general result and give the θ₁ = 90° form U = −pE cos θ.
steps.why: The 90° position is chosen as the zero because there the dipole is sideways to the field and the field does no net work placing it; every other angle is measured against that zero, giving U = −pE cos θ.
common_mistakes: Writing U = −pE sin θ. The stored energy carries cos θ; sin θ belongs to the torque.
Dropping the minus sign in U = −pE cos θ — aligned (θ = 0) must be the LOWEST energy.

recall.must_convey: That the work is stored as U = pE (cos theta-one minus cos theta-two), and from 90 degrees U = minus pE cos theta.
accept: U is pE cos theta one minus cos theta two
minus pE cos theta from ninety degrees
reject: integrate pE sin theta d theta

steps.memory_tip: Zero at 90°: from sideways, turning toward the field releases energy, so aligned is −pE.

insider_note: Torque takes sin θ, energy takes cos θ — the examiner scans for exactly that swap, and for cos θ₁ written before cos θ₂.
